11265.heading: GPS Coarse Acquisition Code
11265.content: The GPS coarse/acquisition code is the shorter civil ranging code used to acquire satellite signals and measure code phase. Each satellite transmits a distinct sequence, enabling a receiver to separate signals that occupy the same carrier frequency. Its unexpectedly strong positioning accuracy helped create a civil market, but that accuracy also led the Defense Department to introduce [[Selective Availability]] as a policy-based degradation rather than redesign the code.

11268.content: GPS aviation navigation replaces dependence on a chain of nearby ground beacons with global three-dimensional position and route guidance. Aviation adoption required more than raw accuracy: users needed integrity, rapid warning of faulty data, dependable coverage, and adequate vertical performance for approach operations. Augmentation systems compare GPS against surveyed ground sites and broadcast corrections and status, allowing smaller airports to gain guidance without installing a complete local precision-approach system.

11280.title: Google Matrix
11280.heading: Google Matrix
11280.content:
The Google matrix is the transition matrix used by the complete [[PageRank]] algorithm. It begins with the web's normalized link structure, repairs rows associated with [[Dangling Node|dangling nodes]], and mixes link-following with [[PageRank Teleportation]].

Every possible move receives a nonzero probability, so repeated multiplication avoids trapped rank and converges to a stable [[PageRank Vector]]. The matrix need not be stored densely; its result can be computed from the sparse hyperlink structure and the teleportation adjustment.

11283.content:
Golden-section search locates a one-dimensional optimum of a unimodal function without derivatives. It maintains a bracketing interval and places interior test points so one previous evaluation can be reused after each reduction.

The constant proportions steadily shrink the interval containing the optimum. The method trades the rapid local convergence of derivative methods for predictable derivative-free progress.

11301.title: GNSS Navigation Message
11301.heading: GNSS Navigation Message
11301.content: A GNSS navigation message is the low-rate data superimposed on a ranging signal. It supplies the transmitting satellite's ephemeris, clock correction and health information, along with broader constellation data that helps a receiver find and assess other satellites. The code phase measures when a signal arrived, while the navigation message provides the orbital and timing context needed to turn that measurement into a position solution.

11304.title: GNSS Interoperability
11304.heading: GNSS Interoperability
11304.content: GNSS interoperability is the ability of independently operated constellations and augmentations to be used together without harmful interference. Shared or coordinated frequency bands and compatible signal structures make common receivers practical, while published relationships among time and coordinate systems support combined solutions. Interoperability improves service and encourages cooperation, yet each provider retains political control and can preserve protected military capabilities.

11307.sourceSearchName: glorot weight initialization glorot weight initialization
11307.title: Glorot Weight Initialization
11307.heading: Glorot Weight Initialization
11307.content:
Glorot initialization samples starting connection weights using a range chosen from the sizes of neighboring layers. Its aim, as Kelleher explains, is to keep the variance of activations moving forward and gradients moving backward at comparable scales across layers.

This is not a weight-training rule. It sets a better starting point before [[Backpropagation]] and [[Gradient Descent]] adjust the weights using data. The book describes its benefit as empirically supported and motivated by variance assumptions, not as a guarantee that every deep model will train successfully. Poor initial scales can worsen the [[Vanishing Gradient Problem]] or make activations and gradients difficult to use.

11316.title: GLONASS
11316.heading: GLONASS
11316.content: GLONASS is the Russian global navigation satellite system developed by the Soviet Union as a counterpart to GPS. Its original design distinguished satellites mainly by carrier frequency rather than the code-division scheme used by GPS. The constellation deteriorated after the Soviet breakup and was later restored to comparable navigation performance. Modern receivers can combine GLONASS with other constellations, and newer generations move toward code-based signal separation.

A global optimum is the best solution among every permitted solution to a problem. It differs from a [[Local Optimum]], which is best only compared with directly neighboring alternatives.

An exact algorithm may guarantee the global optimum but require impractical computation. A heuristic or [[Approximation Algorithm]] can instead seek a good solution efficiently, with the tradeoff stated through bounds or observed performance.

11340.heading: Global and Local Mesh Coordinates
11340.content:
Local mesh coordinates describe a component relative to its object's origin and transform, while global coordinates describe the component's position in the scene. Multiplying a local vertex coordinate by the object's world matrix produces its global position.

The distinction determines whether a geometric test follows the mesh's internal shape or its visible placement. Applying an object's transforms updates local mesh data to incorporate the world placement without visibly moving the object. A location-based algorithm must therefore declare which coordinate system its bounds and comparisons use.

11343.title: Givens Rotation
11343.heading: Givens Rotation
11343.content:
A Givens rotation is an [[Orthogonal Matrix|orthogonal]] transformation that mixes two coordinates while leaving the others unchanged. Its sine and cosine are chosen to zero one selected matrix entry.

Sequences of these rotations can reduce matrices while preserving eigenvalues and norms. They are useful when only a few entries need to be eliminated.

11346.title: Gibbs Sampling
11346.heading: Gibbs Sampling
11346.content:
Gibbs sampling updates one variable at a time by drawing from its conditional distribution given the current values of all other variables. Repeated sweeps construct a Markov chain whose equilibrium distribution is the target joint distribution.

It avoids proposing a complete high-dimensional state at once. Correlated variables can nevertheless make the chain mix slowly, so early samples and strongly dependent runs require careful interpretation.

11349.content: Gibbs free-energy change expresses the part of a reaction's energy that can become reversible electrical work under the stated conditions. The source relates it to enthalpy and entropy by $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$. For a [[Fuel Cell]], $-\Delta G$ sets the maximum work per mole of reaction, while the remainder appears as heat rather than electrical output.

11352.title: Ghosting Visualization
11352.heading: Ghosting Visualization
11352.content:
Ghosting visualization makes selected foreground structure partly transparent or selectively removed so an occluded target can be seen in context. Object-space methods modify a three-dimensional scene representation, while image-space methods operate on projected regions or buffers.

The technique should preserve enough boundary and depth evidence for the viewer to understand which surfaces remain in front. Excessive transparency can make both foreground and hidden information difficult to interpret.

11355.title: Gesture Interaction
11355.heading: Gesture Interaction
11355.content:
Gesture interaction interprets a meaningful movement of the hand, body, or tracked object as a command or spatial input. A gesture may identify an action, indicate an object, describe a path, or manipulate a value.

Recognition must distinguish intentional input from ordinary movement and provide feedback about what was understood. Combining gesture with speech can let one modality name an action while the other supplies spatial arguments.

11358.heading: Gershgorin Circle Theorem

The Gershgorin circle theorem places every eigenvalue of a square matrix inside at least one disk centered at a diagonal entry. The disk radius is the sum of the absolute off-diagonal entries in that row.

These disks bound where eigenvalues can occur before an iterative calculation. Disjoint groups of disks can also reveal how many eigenvalues lie in separated regions.

11370.heading: Geometry-FEM Compatibility
11370.content:
Geometry-FEM compatibility means that imported vertices, edges, faces, and volumes satisfy the receiving solver's requirements for connected domains, entity tolerances, dimension, and meshing. Correct CAD dimensions alone do not establish this compatibility.

Tiny gaps, overlapping entities, sliver faces, and incorrect junctions may be invisible in the authoring tool yet prevent continuity or create poor elements. The FEM specialist must inspect the imported topology in the host environment.

11373.title: Geometry Topology
11373.heading: Geometry Topology
11373.content:
Geometry topology describes how vertices, edges, faces, and volumes connect independently of their exact sizes and curvatures. Two models can look nearly identical yet have different topology if one contains a gap, duplicate edge, disconnected face, or unintended internal boundary.

Finite-element preprocessing depends on this connectivity to form domains and transfer fields continuously across shared entities. Import repair and virtual operations often target topology even when the visible shape changes little.

11375.sourceSearchName: geometry entity selection stability geometry entity selection stability

11376.sourceSearchName: geometry entity selection stability geometry entity selection stability
11376.title: Geometry Entity Selection Stability
11376.heading: Geometry Entity Selection Stability
11376.content:
Geometry entity selection stability is the ability of material, physics, mesh, and boundary assignments to continue identifying the intended regions after a parametric rebuild or import. Explicit numeric entity IDs are fragile because topology changes can renumber them.

Rule-based box, ball, intersection, cumulative, or named selections express the geometric criterion instead of a transient identifier. Stable selection logic makes automated sweeps safer, but every rebuilt model still needs assignment checks.

11379.title: Geometry Symmetry Classes
11379.heading: Geometry Symmetry Classes
11379.content:
Reflectional symmetry reproduces a geometry across a line in two dimensions or a plane in three dimensions. Rotational symmetry reproduces it after a turn about a point or axis; its order states how many repeated sectors complete a full revolution.

Symmetry describes shape before it justifies model reduction. Materials, sources, loads, and boundary conditions must share the same transformation before one repeated portion can represent the rest.

A geometry measurement checkpoint records known distances, areas, volumes, or counts before and after import, repair, simplification, or parameter changes. Agreement within an appropriate tolerance shows that the operation preserved the intended scale and material extent.

The checkpoint belongs in the workflow even when the shape looks simple. Visual inspection alone rarely exposes a uniform scale error, a small missing face, or a Boolean operation that removed the wrong region.

A tolerance set too low leaves defects unrepaired; one set too high merges intended detail or changes boundaries. The value must be chosen relative to model scale and verified against known dimensions and required features after import.

11388.heading: Geometry Dimensionality Reduction
11388.content:
A three-dimensional thermal problem can sometimes be represented in two dimensions when variation along the omitted direction is negligible. Likewise, a long uniform section may permit a one-dimensional treatment along its dominant heat-flow direction.

Axisymmetric geometry retains radial and axial variation while replacing a full body of revolution with a two-dimensional cross-section. Reduction lowers mesh and solver cost, but it is valid only when geometry, materials, sources, and [[Thermal Boundary Condition|conditions]] share the assumed invariance.

11391.heading: Geometry Design Optimization
11391.content:
Geometry design optimization varies dimensions or shape while evaluating an objective under physical and manufacturing constraints. Size optimization changes parameter values, shape optimization moves boundaries, and topology optimization changes where material or connected structure exists.

The objective must be tied to a measurable outcome such as mass, temperature, pressure loss, stress, or cost. A geometrically novel result remains an engineering candidate until its mesh, physics, interfaces, and manufacturability have been checked.

11394.heading: Geometry Build Error Diagnostics
11394.content:
Geometry build error diagnostics use the failed sequence node, highlighted entity, and accompanying message to locate disconnected vertices, overlaps, self-intersections, invalid relationships, or operations that cannot produce a domain. The earliest failing feature is usually more informative than later mesh errors.

Dividing complex assemblies into identifiable regions narrows the search. Repairing or suppressing one feature at a time preserves evidence about which geometric condition caused the failure.

11397.title: Geometric Progression
11397.heading: Geometric Progression
11397.content:
A geometric progression is a [[Sequence]] in which each term after the first is obtained by multiplying by a constant [[Common Ratio]]. The progression

$$6,12,24,48,\ldots$$

has common ratio (2). Unlike the constant additive change of an arithmetic progression, repeated multiplication produces exponential growth or decay. Its direct formula uses a power whose exponent counts the number of ratio applications.

11400.sourceSearchName: geometric hierarchical linkage implementations geometric hierarchical linkage implementations
11400.title: Geometric Hierarchical Linkage Implementations
11400.heading: Geometric Hierarchical Linkage Implementations
11400.content:
Centroid, median, and Ward subclasses implement Lance-Williams recurrences tied to representative geometry or changes in within-cluster dispersion. Their coefficients use cluster sizes and can differ from purely pairwise minimum or maximum rules.

Centroid and median methods may produce nonmonotonic dendrogram inversions, while Ward favors compact variance-minimizing merges. The tree representation preserves the actual join values even when they do not rise monotonically.

11403.title: Geometric Dimension
11403.heading: Geometric Dimension
11403.content:
Geometric dimension identifies the independent spatial directions retained by a model. A point is zero-dimensional, a line or interval is one-dimensional, a planar region is two-dimensional, and a volume is three-dimensional.

Reducing dimension can remove enormous computational cost when variation through an omitted direction is negligible or represented by a property such as thickness or cross-sectional area. The reduction is valid only if the governing physics and boundary conditions remain meaningful in the lower-dimensional representation.

11406.sourceSearchName: geometric clone transformation geometric clone transformation
11406.title: Geometric Clone Transformation
11406.heading: Geometric Clone Transformation
11406.content:
A geometric clone transformation relates the source and pasted regions of a copy-move operation. Simple duplication produces a translation, while an editor may also rotate or scale the copied material to fit a new location.

Matched feature pairs vote for transformation parameters, and a dense cluster of consistent votes identifies a candidate clone. Estimating the transformation also lets the analyst align the regions for pixel-level verification and distinguish one deliberate copy from unrelated repeated patterns.

11407.sourceSearchName: geometric clone transformation geometric clone transformation
11407.title: Geometric Clone Transformation
11407.heading: References

11409.title: Geometric Angle
11409.heading: Geometric Angle
11409.content:
A geometric angle measures the rotation between two rays, lines, directions, or surfaces about a shared origin or intersection. The selected unit and reference direction determine how the same orientation is represented numerically.

Angles enter geometry through sketches, transforms, coordinate systems, work-plane orientation, and boundary relationships. Confusing degrees with radians or reversing the reference direction can create a formally valid but incorrectly oriented model.

11412.title: Geographic Data Exchange Format
11412.heading: Geographic Data Exchange Format
11412.content: A geographic data exchange format serializes geometry, attributes, and often coordinate information so a map can move between software systems. GeoJSON expresses simple geographic features and properties in JSON and can be rendered directly by web tools. KML uses XML to describe geographic content for Earth browsers. Exchange requires checking supported geometry, projection assumptions, attribute types, and file size rather than assuming every spatial object survives unchanged.

11415.heading: Geodetic, Geocentric, and Astronomical Latitude
11415.content: Geocentric latitude uses the line from a surface point to Earth's center, astronomical latitude uses the local direction of gravity, and geodetic latitude uses the normal to the reference ellipsoid. Because Earth is oblate rather than perfectly spherical, these directions generally differ away from the Equator and poles. Unqualified latitude conventionally means geodetic latitude.

11421.heading: Geodetic GPS Surveying
11421.content: Geodetic GPS surveying uses carrier and code observations at known or coordinated stations to determine relative positions far more precisely than a standalone consumer fix. Long observation intervals and differential processing can reduce common satellite, clock, and atmospheric errors to centimeter scale. The resulting measurements support control networks, crustal-motion studies, boundary work, and refinement of the geoid and coordinate datums used to relate orbital positions to the physical Earth.

11424.title: Genomics
11424.heading: Genomics
11424.content:
Genomics studies the complete genetic material of organisms, including sequence, variation, organization, expression, and relationships among genes. It differs from studying one gene in isolation by treating the genome as an interconnected system.

High-throughput instruments and public projects make genomics data-intensive, connecting biological questions to large-scale storage, transfer, analysis, and provenance.

11427.heading: Genomic Data Transfer
11427.content:
Genomic data transfer moves large raw and derived files between instruments, computing centers, repositories, and researchers. Dataset size makes bandwidth, resumable movement, integrity checks, and proximity to computation significant design concerns.

Human genomic data also require authentication, authorization, encryption, and auditable sharing policies during movement.

11430.heading: Genomic Data Storage
11430.content:
Genomic data storage preserves sequences, alignments, variants, annotations, phenotypes, and workflow results at scales that can grow faster than local research infrastructure. Compression and tiered storage reduce cost, but access patterns and reuse determine what must remain readily available.

Retention decisions should distinguish irreplaceable raw observations from derived files that can be reproducibly regenerated.

11433.heading: Genomic Data Analysis
11433.content:
Genomic data analysis turns instrument output into biological claims through quality control, alignment or assembly, variant calling, annotation, comparison, and statistical interpretation. Each stage introduces assumptions and produces intermediate evidence.

Reproducibility requires reference genomes, software versions, parameters, and sample provenance to accompany the final reported variants or associations.

The genomic data life cycle connects acquisition, transfer, storage, analysis, sharing, reuse, and preservation. Decisions at each stage affect later reproducibility, cost, privacy, and scientific interpretation.

Keeping sequence files is insufficient without metadata, reference versions, processing parameters, provenance, access rules, and stable identifiers for derived results.

Metadata must preserve these conditions so technical variation can be distinguished from biological variation.

11445.heading: Genetic K-Modes Selection and Mutation
11445.content:
Selection favors fitter K-modes chromosomes for reproduction, crossover recombines their encoded structure, and mutation introduces categorical changes that preserve exploration. The iteration repeats for a configured number of generations.

Strong selection can collapse diversity prematurely, while excessive mutation turns search into noise. Population size, probabilities, seed, and stopping behavior are therefore part of the algorithm's reproducible configuration.

Genetic K-modes fitness converts within-cluster categorical dissimilarity into a score used to compare chromosomes. Better candidates assign records closer to their corresponding mode and therefore receive greater reproductive influence.

A fitness transformation must remain well behaved when objective values are zero or very similar. The reported final objective should retain its original scale even if selection uses a transformed score.

11451.content:
The genetic K-modes implementation represents a categorical clustering candidate as a chromosome encoding cluster modes or the assignments from which those modes are derived. A population contains several candidates explored concurrently across generations.

The encoding must support efficient distance evaluation and preserve valid categorical values. Initialization diversity gives the search access to alternatives that a single greedy K-modes run might miss.

A genetic algorithm searches with a population of candidate solutions encoded in a manipulable representation. A fitness function selects promising candidates, while mutation and crossover generate a new population for the next iteration.

Repeated selection often finds good solutions to optimization problems whose exhaustive search is intractable. The result is heuristic: success depends on representation, fitness, diversity, and the available computational budget.

11457.heading: Generic Type
11457.content:
A generic type expresses an operation or structure in terms of a type variable supplied by its user. One interface or base service can therefore work with cities, countries, or another model while preserving the specific return type.

Using a type parameter is more informative than replacing every value with an unrestricted type. The generic abstraction captures what the operations share and lets a [[Derived Class]] specialize it.

Generics preserve type safety while reusing a class, struct, interface, or method across multiple types. Compared with storing everything as `object`, a generic parameter avoids routine casts and lets the compiler reject incompatible uses earlier.

11469.heading: Generative Semi-Supervised Classification
11469.content:
Generative semi-supervised classification fits a joint model for features and labels using both labeled and unlabeled observations. Hidden labels on the unlabeled cases are inferred together with distribution parameters.

Expectation-maximization is a natural fitting pattern: infer fractional labels from the current model, then update parameters from both known and inferred assignments. Unlabeled data helps only when the assumed generative family describes the actual feature distribution adequately.

11472.title: Generative Clustering Model
11472.heading: Generative Clustering Model
11472.content:
A generative clustering model describes a mechanism by which a latent cluster first selects a component and that component then generates an observation. Clustering reverses this description to infer likely membership from the observed values.

Because it models the data distribution, it can estimate density, simulate observations, and express overlapping memberships. Its conclusions depend on the assumed component family.

11475.title: Generalizing Specialist
11475.heading: Generalizing Specialist
11475.content:
A generalizing specialist has deep capability in one discipline and enough understanding of adjacent work to collaborate, anticipate constraints, and help outside a narrow role. The person remains a specialist while identifying first with the product team.

This reduces dependency stalls and improves cross-discipline decisions. It does not require every developer to perform every craft at production quality.

11478.title: Generated Ideal
11478.heading: Generated Ideal
11478.content:
The ideal generated by a subset is the smallest ideal containing that subset. In a commutative ring, it consists of finite sums of ring multiples of the generators.

Generated ideals convert specified relations into a quotient in which every generator becomes zero.

11481.content:
The generalized Wilcoxon survival test compares event experience across groups while weighting times by the size of the risk set. It is also known as the Gehan–Breslow test and generally gives greater influence to earlier events than the [[Log-Rank Test]].

Different weighting schemes can lead to different sensitivity when curves separate early or late. The chosen test should match the scientific comparison and be specified before inspecting which weighting gives a smaller p-value.

The generalized reduced gradient method separates variables into dependent and independent groups so equality constraints remain satisfied while the objective improves.

At each iteration it solves constraint equations for dependent-variable changes and uses a reduced gradient to choose movement in the remaining variables. The method repeatedly restores feasibility and searches along a feasible direction.

11487.heading: Generalized Ultrametric
11487.content:
A generalized ultrametric replaces a single non-negative number for a pairwise distance with an element of a partially ordered set, such as a subset of attributes on which two objects differ or a shared-prefix set. The comparison then records structured relationships rather than forcing every distinction onto one scalar scale.

The book connects this view to lattices and formal concept analysis. For binary attribute data, the set-valued relation can expose nested or overlapping concepts directly from the input table, sometimes avoiding construction of every ordinary pairwise distance.

11490.heading: Generalized Mahalanobis Metric Learning
11490.content:
Generalized Mahalanobis metric learning estimates a positive semidefinite matrix that stretches informative directions and contracts unhelpful ones. The resulting distance between two observations is their quadratic difference under that learned matrix.

Because the matrix can be factored into a linear projection, the learned distance is equivalent to ordinary Euclidean distance after transforming the data. Labels or pairwise constraints shape that projection for the classification task.

11493.heading: Generalized Optimal Wavelet Decomposition
11493.content:
Generalized optimal wavelet decomposition selects wavelet-processing choices to produce a useful representation for forecasting. In the source's framework, it is combined with [[Reinforcement Learning]] so the procedure can search for decomposition and thresholding decisions that improve predictive performance.

The method illustrates automated analytics as a coordinated pipeline: transform the signal, suppress noise, fit a learner, and compare in-sample and out-of-sample results.

11496.title: General Term of an Arithmetic Progression
11496.heading: General Term of an Arithmetic Progression
11496.content:
The general term of an arithmetic progression gives its value at position (n) without listing earlier terms. If the first term is (a_1) and the [[Common Difference]] is (d), then

$$a_n=a_1+d(n-1).$$

The factor (n-1) appears because no difference has yet been added at the first position. For (2,7,12,17,\ldots), the formula is (2+5(n-1)). Setting this expression equal to a proposed value tests whether that value occurs at a natural-number position.

11499.heading: Generalized Label Propagation
11499.content:
Generalized label propagation spreads label or membership information across a graph under smoothness and constraint objectives. Labeled vertices anchor the process while nearby unlabeled vertices acquire compatible scores.

Extensions can handle multiple classes, soft labels, negative relations, and heterogeneous graphs. If the graph reflects nuisance similarity, propagation confidently amplifies the wrong relation, making graph construction and uncertainty reporting essential.

11502.heading: General Term of a Geometric Progression
11502.content:
The general term of a geometric progression gives the value at position (n) from the first term (a_1) and [[Common Ratio]] (r):

$$a_n=a_1r^{n-1}.$$

The exponent is (n-1) because the first term has not yet been multiplied by the ratio. For (6,12,24,48,\ldots), the formula is (6\cdot2^{n-1}). This expression condenses repeated multiplication and permits any position to be evaluated directly.

11505.title: Gaze Awareness
11505.heading: Gaze Awareness
11505.content:
Gaze awareness is the ability of collaborators to understand where another participant is looking or directing attention. In person this is partly conveyed by head and eye orientation; mediated AR may need to preserve or explicitly visualize the cue.

Knowing a partner's focus helps resolve references such as “this part” and coordinates turn-taking around shared objects. Approximate gaze can be useful, but the interface should not imply more measurement precision than the tracker provides.

11508.title: Gaussian Mixture EM Implementation
11508.heading: Gaussian Mixture EM Implementation
11508.content:
The GMC class implements expectation-maximization for Gaussian mixture clustering. The expectation step computes component responsibilities from current weights, means, and covariance matrices; the maximization step re-estimates those parameters from the responsibilities.

Iteration monitors log-likelihood change and stops at a tolerance or iteration limit. Responsibilities support soft inference internally, while the published membership vector selects the most probable component for each record.

11511.heading: Gene Expression Biclustering
11511.content:
Gene-expression biclustering searches for a subset of genes that behaves coherently across a subset of experimental conditions. It does not require the same gene relationship to hold across the entire matrix.

Biclusters can overlap because a gene may participate in different processes under different conditions. Objectives may seek constant, additive, multiplicative, or order-preserving patterns, so the coherence model shapes the biological claim.

11514.heading: Gaussian Mixture Model
11514.content:
A Gaussian mixture model combines several normal distributions, each with its own mean, covariance, and mixture weight. The components create regions of increased density interpreted as clusters.

Covariance determines each cluster's volume, orientation, and ellipsoidal shape. Probabilistic memberships allow the component regions to overlap.

11517.title: Gaussian Elimination
11517.heading: Gaussian Elimination
11517.content:
Gaussian elimination uses [[Elementary Row Operation|row operations]] to transform an [[Augmented Matrix]] into upper triangular or [[Row Echelon Form]]. The resulting system is completed by [[Back Substitution]].

A small or zero pivot can amplify error or halt the naive algorithm. [[Partial Pivoting]] and [[Scaled Partial Pivoting]] rearrange rows to improve reliability.

After assembly and boundary-condition enforcement, a finite element model becomes a simultaneous linear system. Gaussian elimination provides a direct route to its nodal unknowns by triangularization followed by back substitution.

11520.title: Gaussian Membership Function
11520.heading: Gaussian Membership Function
11520.content:
A Gaussian membership function assigns maximum membership at a center and decreases smoothly according to a bell-shaped curve controlled by its spread. It provides a differentiable representation without sharp corners.

The center states the prototype value and the width determines how quickly membership fades. Overlapping Gaussian functions can encode ordered fuzzy categories.
